title: Type I and type II errors; statistical power

videos.script: A test makes a decision, and a decision can be wrong. There are exactly two ways. {{two}} The first: nothing is going on, and the test says something is. A false alarm. Statisticians call it a type one error, and its chance is the significance level, five percent. You chose that. {{type1}} The second: something real is going on, and the test misses it. A type two error. Its chance has no fixed value. It depends on how big the effect is and how much data you collected. {{type2}} Horta's routing trial is the example. Twenty-five deliveries, no significant result. Suppose the new system really saves two minutes a delivery. How likely was the trial to notice? {{suppose}} The answer is about one chance in two. A coin toss. The trial was too small to have a fair chance of finding what it was looking for. {{coin}} That chance of finding a real effect is called power. This lesson computes it, shows how to plan a study with enough of it, and shows a strange thing that happens when underpowered studies do find something: they exaggerate it. {{power}}
